यूपी: प्रदेश में अब बदलने लगा मौसम, रात के पारे में गिरावट और सुबह-शाम भी बढ़ी ठंडक; सबसे ठंडा रहा ये जिला
उत्तर प्रदेश में रात के तापमान में गिरावट से सुबह और शाम ठंडक बढ़ने लगी है। मौसम वैज्ञानिक अतुल कुमार सिंह के अनुसार, आने वाले दिनों में रात का पारा दो डिग्री सेल्सियस तक और गिर सकता है। सोमवार को अयोध्या सबसे ठंडा रहा, जबकि हरदोई और नजीबाबाद में न्यूनतम तापमान 16 डिग्री दर्ज हुआ।
विस्तार
उत्तर प्रदेश में अब रात के तापमान में गिरावट शुरू हो गई है। सुबह-शाम और रात में हल्की ठंडक महसूस होने लगी है। पश्चिमी यूपी के बरेली, मेरठ, मुजफ्फरनगर समेत करीब आधा दर्जन जिलों में तो दिन का तापमान भी सामान्य से एक से दो डिग्री सेल्सियस कम रहा।
क्षेत्रीय मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र के वरिष्ठ वैज्ञानिक अतुल कुमार सिंह ने बताया कि आने वाले दिनों में रात के तापमान में दो डिग्री सेल्सियस तक और गिरावट हो सकती है। इससे दिन में मौसम सुहाना रहेगा, जबकि सुबह और रात की ठंडक बढ़ेगी।
अयोध्या में सबसे ठंडा दिन
सोमवार को 29 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान के साथ अयोध्या प्रदेश में सबसे ठंडा रहा। वहीं हरदोई और नजीबाबाद दोनों जिलों में न्यूनतम तापमान 16 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया। यहां प्रदेश में सबसे ठंडी रात रही।
गिरने लगा रात का पारा
राजधानी के मौसम में स्थिरता आने लगी है। दिन चढ़ने के साथ धूप खिली, हालांकि इसकी तपिश नरम रही। वहीं, रात के तापमान में हल्की गिरावट शुरू हो गई है। क्षेत्रीय मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र, लखनऊ के वरिष्ठ वैज्ञानिक अतुल कुमार सिंह ने बताया कि अगले एक सप्ताह तक मौसम शुष्क रहने के आसार हैं।
इस दौरान दिन के तापमान में करीब दो डिग्री की बढ़ोतरी, जबकि रात के तापमान में दो से तीन डिग्री की गिरावट हो सकती है। इससे सुबह और रात में हल्की ठंडक महसूस होने लगेगी।रविवार को अधिकतम तापमान लगभग स्थिर रहते हुए 32.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया। वहीं, न्यूनतम तापमान 0.7 डिग्री की गिरावट के साथ 21.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा।

full_text:
AsianScientist (Oct. 19, 2026) –Of the 50 most polluted cities in the world in 2025, 29 are in India. It is well-known that poor air quality traps heat and contributes to the rising temperature in the region. Now, researchers from Hong Kong Baptist University have found that the country’s extreme heat might also be making its air even more polluted, creating a dangerous feedback loop.
Their study, published in Advances in Atmospheric Sciences, also details how an anomalous weather pattern fuels the feedback loop in India’s northern region.
Combined with rising temperatures, this helps explain why northern India has been experiencing more days of concurrent heat waves and severe air pollution, known as co-extreme days.
“Most studies have focused on heat waves and air pollution separately,” said lead author Huibin Dai of Hong Kong Baptist University. “This study shows that large-scale atmospheric circulation can simultaneously intensify heat and promote secondary aerosol formation.”
Before 2020, the number of co-extreme days in India was actually declining. After 2020, however, the trend reversed.
Delhi, a densely populated city in northern India, experienced extreme heat and severe air pollution on more than half of the days in April 2022. From 2017 to 2024, the city recorded a total of 388 co-extreme days.
The researchers investigated whether the increase in human emissions after the pandemic could explain why co-extreme days have become more frequent. To find out, the team analyzed satellite observations and air quality monitoring data from 2017 to 2024, then simulated a scenario in which human emissions remained at 2017 levels while chemical and meteorological processes changed from year to year.
The simulations reproduced much of the observed changes in air pollution and temperature, which suggests that meteorological and chemical factors might be playing significant roles.
During extreme heat, concentrations of tiny organic carbon particles in the atmosphere rose to as much as 2.3 times their average levels. These concentrations were even higher on co-extreme days than on days when air pollution was high but temperatures were normal.
Unlike smoke and dust particles which are emitted directly into the air, organic carbon forms through chemical reactions in the atmosphere. Heat accelerates these reactions, producing more particles that contribute to air pollution.
This effect is compounded by anticyclonic circulation, a weather pattern that occurs particularly in northern India. It causes air to sink and spread outward near the ground, restricting vertical airflow. As a result, heat and pollutants accumulate near the surface rather than dispersing into the upper atmosphere.
The findings highlight how atmospheric chemistry and weather patterns can interact to shape air quality during extreme heat events, with potential consequences for public health.
“The next step is to investigate how compound extremes will evolve under future climate change and to quantify their impacts on human health,” Dai said. “Ultimately, this work aims to provide scientific evidence to support early prevention, risk reduction, and climate adaptation.”
—
Source: Institute of Atmospheric Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences ; Image: amnat30/shutterstock
The study can be found at: Revival of Compound Heat–PM2.5 Extremes in Pre-Monsoon India: Meteorological Shifts and Fueled Secondary Aerosol Production (2017–24)

full_text:
Raichur (Karnataka) [India], October 19 (ANI): Even as the monsoon season has set in, scorching heat continues to prevail, keeping the demand for tender coconuts high and pushing prices up to Rs 80 per coconut in Raichur city.
Usually, demand for tender coconut peaks during summer. However, this year, inadequate rainfall and persistent high temperatures have sustained the demand even during the monsoon. The refreshing drink that offers relief from the heat is now burning a hole in consumers’ pockets.
With temperatures soaring, people are turning to tender coconut water to keep themselves cool. Shortage in supply coupled with high demand has led to a sharp price hike.
In Raichur city, small-sized tender coconuts are being sold at Rs 50 to Rs 60, while medium-sized coconuts are priced between Rs 70 and Rs 80, leaving consumers to bear the double burden of heat and price rise.
There are around 40 tender coconut vendors in Raichur city, of which four to five are wholesale traders. Each truckload brings approximately 6,000 tender coconuts to the city.
Tender coconuts are supplied to Raichur from Maddur in Mandya district. Wholesale traders purchase a medium-sized coconut for Rs 55 to Rs 60 and sell it to local vendors for Rs 62 to Rs 65. The vendors then retail the same coconut to consumers for Rs 70 to Rs 80.
Earlier, truckloads arrived once every two days. However, vendors say supplies have now dropped to just twice a week. Transportation of large quantities of tender coconuts to cities like Mumbai and Delhi is also said to be affecting local supply.
“Due to lack of rainfall, heat has increased, and tender coconut prices have also gone up. We are currently selling them for Rs 70 to Rs 80 each. Prices may rise further in the coming days. Despite the increase, the number of customers has not decreased,” said Ganesh, a tender coconut vendor.
Vendors believe tender coconut production has declined due to inadequate rainfall across the state, while consumption has increased due to the heat, resulting in a supply-demand mismatch.
Consumers say tender coconuts, which were available at lower prices during monsoon and winter earlier, have now become expensive.
“Because of intense heat, drinking tender coconut water has become necessary. However, it used to be available at a much lower price, whereas now it costs Rs 70 to Rs 80. This has become a financial burden for ordinary people. A reduction in prices would be a great relief,” said Mahendra Mitra, a consumer.
Those who consume it for health reasons, patients who drink it on medical advice, and fitness enthusiasts continue to buy it regardless of the price, said another consumer, Vinay Kumar.
Overall, inadequate rainfall, rising temperatures and fluctuations in supply have pushed up tender coconut prices. Whether prices will come down in the coming days with the arrival of rainfall, a drop in temperatures and improvement in supply remains to be seen. (ANI)

How Peterborough and other municipalities are adapting to extreme heat
As Peterborough plans for the impacts of climate change, an innovative strategy in BC tries to protect vulnerable renters
A mass of warm air rolled in over British Columbia in late June 2021 and then became trapped there, unmoving, for a full week. The province reached the hottest temperature ever recorded in Canada and then broke the record again the very next day, peaking at 47.9 degrees C (118 degrees F) in Lytton, BC on June 28.
Emergency switchboards and hospitals were overrun. By the time the heat broke just after Canada Day, at least 619 people were dead, and the province was left reeling by a new kind of crisis.
“Our bodies aren’t meant to operate under these kinds of temperatures,” explains Deanna Leahy, public health promoter at Lakelands Public Health. She notes that excess temperatures can lead to heat exhaustion and heat stroke, and are particularly dangerous for people with pre-existing health conditions. “The way that it stresses the body, and especially stresses the heart. People with heart health conditions, respiratory conditions, or kidney-related diseases are at greater risk.”
Indeed, a coroner’s report prepared after the BC heat dome notes that two-thirds of the deaths were seniors and 80 per cent had chronic illnesses. Leahy notes that pregnant people, children, and people on certain medications are also particularly susceptible to the heat.
Peterborough hasn’t yet experienced a heat event as extreme as the 2021 BC heat dome, though it has seen its fair share of climate change-related extreme weather events in recent years, including the 2022 derecho and the 2025 ice storm. While the summer of 2026 turned out to be relatively mild in Peterborough, summer heat is trending higher. By the 2050s, models suggest that Peterborough will see at least 26 days where temperatures spike beyond 30 degrees C, every summer.
“In 2021 in BC, we could honestly say that we didn’t see it coming,” says Nadine Nakagawa, city councillor in New Westminster, BC. “When the next heat dome comes – when, not if – we cannot say again that we didn’t know and we weren’t prepared. We know it’s coming, so we have to take action.”
In BC, the heat dome became a catalyst for new legislation and innovative strategies to protect vulnerable people impacted by climate change, including new, first-of-its-kind rules for landlords that protect renters by setting maximum safe indoor temperatures in rental units.
As climate scientists announce that we’ve crossed the threshold for at least a 1.5-degree rise in global temperatures, Peterborough’s government and public health authorities are seeking new, local responses to an increasingly hotter globe.
The local weather response network
On June 29, 2026, as Peterborough entered its first multi-day heat event of the year, the city put out a media release, Staying Cool as Temperatures Soar, listing city facilities where residents could go to cool down. It included public buildings, splashpads, beaches, and water refill stations, and also directed people towards the city’s interactive Cooling Spaces Interactive Map, with the same information. At the same time, an alert went out on Alertable, a free mobile app that the city uses to notify citizens of important updates and pass along weather alerts.
“In emergency management, there’s a lot of coordination,” says Brea Keeling, advisor in the city’s Emergency and Risk Management Division, who were responsible for these public releases. Her division has been developing “hazard-specific plans that we use as guiding documents for our responses,” but it can be difficult because “events are fluid and fast-changing, so we can’t just have a one-thing-fits-all solution,” meaning that local authorities rely on partner agencies to guide their work.
“We work closely with Emergency Management Ontario,” says Keeling. “Any of the weather alerts that are released, we typically have a meeting with Environment and Climate Change. From there, as city emergency management representatives, we can create and coordinate media releases to provide updates.”
A local network of organizations, the Extreme Temperature Network, is also activated during these periods. Spearheaded by Lakelands Public Health, the group also includes representatives from the city government as well as other community partners, who meet during extreme heat events as well as on an ongoing basis.
“We come together every two or three months,” says Deanna Leahy. “It’s an opportunity for Public Health and all of the members to share information, questions, and experiences from different weather events that these community agency reps can bring forward from their population.”
She notes that the group includes non-profits that serve populations that are known to be particularly vulnerable during extreme heat events, like unhoused people and senior citizens, and has resulted in an “agency toolkit that incorporates some of the learning and information from the network.”
The Extreme Temperature Network is a newer addition to the city’s emergency response, organized out of recommendations put out in the 2020 City of Peterborough Community Climate Change Resiliency Strategy, one of the most comprehensive assessments to date of the possible effects of climate change in our community.

Gauteng residents have been urged to take precautions as the province experiences extreme heat.
The province is experiencing its first official heatwave of the 2026/27 summer season, with temperatures expected to soar until Monday.
Temperatures
According to Gauteng Weather, the heatwave, which began on Friday, was forecast to intensify on Sunday, bringing scorching conditions across the province.
Pretoria is expected to be the hottest, reaching a sweltering 35°C, while Johannesburg is forecast to hit 33°C and Vereeniging 32°C.
A heatwave with persistently high temperatures is also expected over parts of the Mpumalanga Highveld, the southern Mpumalanga Lowveld and the south-western bushveld of Limpopo.
Warning
Health experts warn that prolonged exposure to extreme heat can increase the risk of dehydration, heat exhaustion and heatstroke, particularly among vulnerable groups such as children, the elderly and people with underlying health conditions.
Residents have been encouraged to stay hydrated by drinking plenty of water throughout the day and avoiding drinks that can contribute to dehydration, including alcohol and excessive amounts of coffee.

Will employers be able to force people to work during a “yellow” alert: new rules take effect on December 4
Kyiv • UNN
Starting December 4, businesses without shelters will not be allowed to operate during a yellow alert. The consent of the workforce will no longer replace protection.
Starting December 4, businesses without shelters will not be able to operate during a "yellow" air-raid alert. On that day, the transition period will end, during which businesses without shelters may continue operating with the approval of the workforce. After that date, to operate in the normal mode, businesses must provide employees and visitors with adequate protection.
What this will mean for employers and workers in practice was examined by UNN.
What rules currently apply during an air-raid alert
Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 1092 of September 4, 2026, introduced differentiated notification of air threats. The "yellow" level means a drone threat, while the "red" level means a missile, missile-and-drone, or massive drone threat.
During the "yellow" level, businesses may continue operating if the facility has a protective structure, temporary or permanent shelter, a dual-purpose structure, or an equipped safe space. These requirements apply to business entities regardless of their form of ownership. For businesses without shelters, the government provided three months for preparation, so until December 4 they may operate during a drone threat with the approval of the workforce. A manager’s order alone is insufficient for this. However, after the transition period ends, employees’ consent will no longer replace the necessary protective measures.
What will be considered a safe space for work after December 4
It will not always be necessary to build a separate permanent shelter to enable people to work safely and ensure that the employer does not violate the law. Resolution No. 1128 allows, in specified cases, a safe space to be arranged directly inside a building. At the same time, an ordinary corridor or windowless room will not automatically become a shelter. The matter concerns the most protected areas capable of shielding people from the secondary effects of weapons and from a specified level of blast-wave overpressure. Compliance of the premises with these requirements must be substantiated by specific calculations.
In addition, the employer must determine the procedure for staff actions during an alert and ensure the timely notification of employees and visitors. At the entrance, on the exterior wall, or on the fence of the facility, a sign measuring 100 by 60 centimeters must be placed, stating whether a shelter or safe space is available or absent.
Can an employee refuse dangerous work during an air-raid alert
Even if the workforce has approved working during a "yellow" air-raid alert, this does not deprive an individual employee of the right to refuse an assignment that threatens their life or health. This right is established by Article 6 of the Law of Ukraine "On Labor Protection." However, for the refusal to have legal effect, the worker must immediately inform their supervisor about the danger.
What will change for businesses after December 4
If a business does not arrange adequate protection, it will not be able to justify continuing normal operations during a "yellow" danger level solely by referring to the workforce’s consent. In the absence of a shelter or safe space, operations will have to be suspended for the duration of such a threat, except in cases for which the government has established a separate procedure.
If employees are injured during an attack, the circumstances of the incident and the employer’s fulfillment of occupational safety obligations will be investigated. Of course, the mere fact that the Russian Armed Forces struck the business will not be attributed as the fault of its management. However, collective approval will not relieve management of liability for violating safety rules during work.
To recap
In mid-September, Ukraine established rules for railway operations during an air threat. At the yellow level, trains may operate and passengers may board. At the red level, boarding is suspended and people are moved to shelters.
